query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using simultaneous in-situ XRD and TGA at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–1200 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere will reveal real-time phase transformations and mass changes of a high-entropy alloy, enabling accurate determination of its oxidation behavior and phase stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy in as-cast form.
generation.intervention: Perform in-situ X-ray diffraction and thermogravimetric analysis concurrently during thermal exposure in an oxidizing environment.
generation.conditions: Ramp temperature from ambient to 1100 ± 50 °C under controlled oxygen partial pressure; hold for up to several hours while continuously collecting diffraction and mass data.
generation.structural_mediator: Real-time phase formation (e.g., new oxide phases) monitored by XRD and correlated with TGA-measured mass changes.
generation.mechanism: In-situ diffraction detects emergent oxide Bragg peaks and tracks the transformation from the FCC parent phase, while TGA quantifies the mass gains associated with oxidation, clarifying the kinetics and pathways of scale formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable, time-dependent mass increase in TGA that correlates directly with the appearance and growth of oxides in XRD patterns, reflecting oxidation progression and phase evolution.
generation.baseline: Ex-situ oxidation tests and post-exposure phase identification via XRD without real-time tracking.
generation.boundary: Limited to temperatures below approximately 1400 °C and to conditions where the sample and instrumentation remain stable. Oxidation processes requiring very high pressure or extended times may need additional methods.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative analysis of minor phases requires careful calibration to avoid errors in phase fraction estimation; extrapolation to non-air environments remains less certain.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct simultaneous TGA and in-situ XRD on replicate CrMnFeCoNi samples over the 700–1100 °C range in air (or controlled oxygen) for multiple dwell times. Monitor weight change and XRD patterns at set intervals or continuously.
measurements: Real-time XRD scans to detect new diffraction peaks or peak shifts
Post-experimental microstructural analysis of oxide layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured mass gain by TGA does not correspond to the emergence of new phases in the in-situ XRD data, or if no new oxide phases are observed despite significant oxidation, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
